source_title: Hertz Global Holdings, Inc. Form 8-K Exhibit 99.2 (Chapter 11 plan emergence press release), FY2021
publisher_issuer: Hertz Global Holdings, Inc. (SEC EDGAR CIK 0001657853)
company_context: Hertz Global Holdings, the asset-heavy car-rental operator, filed for Chapter 11 in May 2020 after the COVID-19 collapse in travel demand caused a sudden revenue shock against a debt-and-fleet-financing-heavy balance sheet. A joint plan of reorganization was confirmed June 10, 2021 and became effective June 30, 2021, allowing the company to emerge from bankruptcy.
business_type: Asset-heavy car rental; large vehicle fleet financed through asset-backed (ABS) facilities and corporate debt
evidence_summary: Hertz filed Chapter 11 in May 2020 when travel demand collapsed: at the start of proceedings roughly $6.0 billion of indebtedness was automatically accelerated and approximately $13.5 billion of additional third-party indebtedness was triggered by defaults and termination events (~$19.5 billion of debt obligations affected). The business itself remained viable once demand recovered. The confirmed plan (effective June 30, 2021) eliminated over $5 billion of debt (including all of Hertz Europe's corporate debt), provided payment in cash in full to creditors, and left existing shareholders with more than $1 billion of value. Hertz emerged with a new $2.8 billion exit credit facility (at least $1.3 billion of term loans plus a revolver) and an approximately $7 billion asset-backed vehicle financing facility, funded by a roughly $6 billion plan-sponsor investment from Knighthead, Certares, and Apollo.

source_backed_metrics.exit_credit_facility_usd: $2.8 billion (at least $1.3 billion term loans plus revolver)

outcome_evidence: Plan of reorganization confirmed June 10, 2021 and effective June 30, 2021; eliminated over $5 billion of debt, paid creditors in cash in full, and delivered more than $1 billion of value to existing shareholders, completing emergence from Chapter 11.

why_useful_for_opsiq: A clean example of a temporary exogenous shock (travel collapse) interacting with a leveraged, asset-heavy fleet structure to force bankruptcy, followed by a genuine recovery and emergence. Useful for testing OpsIQ's ability to distinguish a survivable shock (outcome 13) from terminal decline, and to model adaptive re-evaluation when a shock event hits a debt_solvency_pressure / strategic_capex_risk profile.
